Besides a big update for phones, there’s also a sizable Pixel Watch Drop today, but it’s mostly a preview of what’s to come.

Like on phones and Googlebooks, Create My Widget lets you create custom displays of information on the Pixel Watch 4 and newer.

Manual Call Screen is becoming Gemini Call Screen on the Pixel Watch 5. This “proactive, agentic feature” will filter incoming calls on demand and generate key details in US English.

The final feature lets your nearby phone unlock the Pixel Watch instead of having to manually enter the PIN or pattern on a small screen. After unlocking your phone, a prompt (“Unlocking your watch”) appears at the top of the screen with a button to “Cancel.” Your watch must be on your wrist to unlock. As more information about the ongoing situation at Nvidia unravels, U.S. President Donald Trump has confirmed that the FBI is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy days after he admitted to the indiscretion. According to the Associated Press, the president said this during a briefing at the White House, with one reporter asking him about his knowledge of Huang’s issue before it became publicly known. The news comes amidst a separate bombshell report from Bloomberg, which claims that Nvidia intervened in a US government probe of suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was an executive.

“Well, I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading about it over a period of time, but, uh, not too long ago,” Trump said. “We’ll look into, I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something, and I think he’ll be in good shape.” He also said, “I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how you’re doing. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

It has been previously reported that U.S. intelligence services suspected that Alice Huang, who previously held an executive position at Megaspeed, had ties to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is one of the country’s intelligence services, and that they told the President about it over a year ago. However, it was reported he did not act on the information, as he reportedly did not want to jeopardize Nvidia sales or antagonize Beijing, especially after the White House approved the export of H200 chips to China with an attached 25% fee.

Congress has called Huang once to confront him about these rumors, with the CEO confirming his affair with Alice Huang shortly after. The committee said it has "concerns over Nvidia’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company.” Now, it seems that the FBI, which is the U.S.’s primary domestic counterintelligence agency, is looking into the situation, too.

While the infidelity of tech executives is usually outside the purview of politicians and law enforcement, Jensen Huang’s sensitive position as the head of the leading AI chip manufacturer that arguably single-handedly drove the global AI race has made him a prominent target. China has denied the accusation that Alice Huang is its agent, but a think tank suggests that “China is employing ‘attractive women’ posing as investors, business professionals, academics, or romantic partners to gain access to U.S. tech talent, networks, and research infrastructure.”

This is why Nvidia’s supposed intervention in the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security’s (BIS) investigation into Megaspeed is becoming a concern. Megaspeed has been investigated for allegedly smuggling $2 billion worth of Nvidia AI processors into China, although Nvidia has claimed that it has done its due diligence and did not find any signs of diversions by the company. Despite that, Bloomberg reports that Nvidia executive vice president and general counsel Tim Teter reached out to U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security and BIS head Jeffrey Kessler to ask about the administration’s investigation into the company and whether the BIS was involved in Singapore’s detention of Alice Huang at that time. Sources claimed that the U.S. agency was not involved in Ms. Huang’s apprehension by Singaporean authorities.

The publication reported BIS staff were told to route all Nvidia requests through Kessler or to seek approval from him for any outreach involving the company, which people say was highly unusual, and that Teter even supposedly reached out directly to BIS employees. When the affected employees forwarded the emails to Kessler and raised their concerns, the BIS chief instructed them to handle the case by the book. But in late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working alongside the BIS, asked the bureau to pause its efforts on the Megaspeed investigation.

#10400. The success KPIs nonprofits get right

Most organizations are built around a simple equation: Build a business, generate revenue, grow. I spent much of my career working within that equation, where success is often measured by familiar numbers: customers, dollars, CAGR.

Nonprofits start from a different premise. Their purpose is to advance a mission. And I have long argued that the clearest missions rarely have a true endpoint. An organization can work toward its goal for decades without ever being able to say, “We’re done.”

Measuring success can be more complex for nonprofits than for for-profit organizations. But in my work with the iF Design Foundation, a German nonprofit, I have found the opposite can also be true. When there is no ultimate finish line, you must be more intentional about why you do the work and how progress and success get measured.

A CLEAR PURPOSE MAKES DECISIONS SIMPLER

When growth is the primary objective, almost any decision can be justified so long as it pushes profits in an upward trajectory. Aaron Sorkin’s recent film depiction of Meta, The Social Reckoning, offers one take on what happens when that logic goes unchecked. But when the mission is the destination, a different question comes into focus: Does this decision support what we are ultimately here to achieve?

That question does not make difficult decisions easier, but it gives a clearer framework for making them.

I saw this firsthand when iF Design updated one of its annual iF DESIGN AWARD criteria three years back. We replaced the previous “Impact” criterion, which also included commercial considerations, with “Sustainability,” a framework tailored to the most relevant social and environmental factors in each of the award’s design categories. The criterion accounts for one-fifth of the total entry score, making iF the only international design award known to fully integrate these factors into its primary jurying criteria.

Changing an established system required rethinking the underlying jurying premise of “what makes great design?” and bringing sustainability experts from across disciplines and around the world into the process. There were logistical challenges and questions about implementation. Keeping the existing system would have been simpler. But our mission gave us a clear reason to move forward.

iF exists to advance design excellence and impact. If we believe design has a role to play in creating a better future for all, then sustainability invariably is part of how we evaluate it. The decision was not necessarily the easiest one. It was simply the decision most consistent with pursuing our purpose at this moment in time.

WITH NO ENDPOINT, DEFINE PROGRESS YOURSELF

In most for-profit companies, the scoreboard is largely handed to you. There may be debate over which numbers matter most, and differences based on ownership structures, industry, geography, etc., but the broad measures of success are usually understood.

A mission without a finish line comes with no such scoreboard. You have to decide what progress looks like.

I have found that more useful than disorienting. At iF, I think about growth less in terms of the organization’s size and more in terms of how many people engage with and are positively affected by its mission. Each year, tens of thousands of designers from around the world submit work to iF Design’s various award programs. But the number of entries matters less than what that participation makes possible: new ideas, objective feedback, and talent recognition, for starters.

This is a more strategic way to think about growth. The question is not simply whether the numbers are going up, but who is benefiting from our work.

WHAT FOR-PROFITS AND NONPROFITS CAN LEARN FROM EACH OTHER

Having spent years on both sides, I do not believe one model is inherently better. They serve different purposes and bring different offerings to the world. But after years as a senior marketer and operator focused on values-based brand building across the two, I would like to see the for-profit world start learning from the nonprofit world.

It all starts with purpose. A buzzword, yes, but fundamentally it is the question of “Why do we exist, and to what end?”

Purpose should not be an idea articulated after the business case has already been made. It should help determine whether the business case makes sense in the first place. For brand builders, that means treating mission and values as a starting point for decision-making, not simply as marketing messages. Done well, this approach can also strengthen brand loyalty and customer advocacy.

That is perhaps the biggest shift in perspective the nonprofit model has given me. Because in the for-profit world, nearly every problem depends on the answer to the question, “Will this grow the business?”

This is not to imply that revenue, profit, and growth are unimportant. Every organization needs to create enough value to sustain itself, and nonprofits are no exception. But when purpose is clear, money becomes a means rather than the primary destination.

When you understand what growth makes possible for the people you serve and the wider world, it becomes much easier to know whether you are moving in the right direction.

Lisa Gralnek is U.S. managing director and global head of sustainability at iF DESIGN, and host of the award-winning podcast FUTURE OF XYZ.

It would certainly be a welcome development for open-source projects everywhere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most open-source projects have meager resources, and the inrush of AI-provided bug reports and "fixes" has been a bane on their respective maintainers. However, the Linux kernel is well-manned, and code for it generally has a higher barrier to entry than in other places. Linus Torvalds thinks that the flood of AI bug reports may be settling, as the kernel's Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) portion saw more AI fixes than reports.

Torvalds splits off the changes among three areas: graphics, networking, and sound drivers; networking and the BPF; and miscellaneous changes. He proceeds to state that "much of this was driven by various AI fixes," an apparent underscoring of his stance that AI-written contributions should be embraced rather than shunned — so long as they're subject to the same quality control.

The Linux maestro also relayed a note from Alexei Starovoitov, the BPF maintainer, who claims that this subsection actually saw a higher rate of AI-provided fixes versus reports. This might signal a tidal shift, at least where the Linux kernel is concerned, and would be exceedingly welcome news for other open-source maintainers everywhere tired of dealing with junk reports at the same time they have to handle a higher influx of legitimate bugs, thanks to AI-driven bug discovery.

In Torvalds' own words, "I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we may be starting to see the tide starting to turn."

Anyone can make a pointless bug report, but it's hard to deny that the existence of powerful AI bots has prompted a renewed focus on cybersecurity most everywhere. Firefox fixed 423 security bugs in an April release, Chrome found and fixed 1,072 bugs in June — making for more fixes in 2026 than the project's previous eight years — and my personal "favorite," NodeJS, sadly fixed 50 vulnerabilities instead of announcing its closure.

Many open-source projects have complained about high-volume, low-quality AI-driven bug reports, with some even shutting down their bug bounty programs altogether, or placing additional verifications for issue reports. We'd venture that the Linux kernel has a much larger bug-triaging team than your average project, though, meaning it has more resources to sift through the junk.

This tentative conclusion popped up in a message sent yesterday to the kernel mailing list, wherein Torvalds briefly describes the overall shape of the kernel's 7.4-rc2 update. He says that despite the update looking large from a pure file-count perspective, it's actually mostly composed of one- and two-line fixes and is "very straightforward" to implement.

#10396. ‘You’ve Got Mail’ is getting a remake. There’s just one problem with that: Everything!

There are plenty of reasons to not remake a movie. Maybe it’s a stone-cold classic that seemingly can’t be improved upon. Sometimes it’s a foreign film that worked well enough already without photoshopping American faces into the lead roles. Other times, it’s an older movie with a recognizable title that nobody actually cares about anymore or one made so recently that remaking it serves no discernible purpose. These are all legitimate critiques, yet studios enamored with intellectual property frequently ignore them—with varying artistic and box office success.

You’ve Got Mail is a different situation altogether. 

While it’s perhaps impossible to replicate the star wattage, irresistible charm, and effortless chemistry of 1998 Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan, or the whip-smart comedic precision of filmmaker Nora Ephron (RIP), that isn’t even the main strike against a remake. Never mind that You’ve Got Mail reunited this trio five years after their funny, tearjerking smash, Sleepless in Seattle, giving it the rom-com equivalent of a Marvel movie’s magnitude. What makes You’ve Got Mail uniquely un-remake-able is that technology, social norms, and economics have changed so much in the last 28 years that everything about this movie now feels like a relic of the distant past.

Gen Z moviegoers—currently, the most active and coveted demographic—have likely never even heard the AOL notification that lent You’ve Got Mail its name. (It finally faded away for good last year when AOL discontinued its dial-up internet service, but the audio file had fallen out of cultural relevance sometime in the early-aughts.) If the words “You’ve got mail” now mean anything to young people, it’s likely in the context of “That old movie my parents like.”

An extremely 1998 film

Title aside, not much is known about the new Warner Bros. project. It will be directed by Jason Orley, the creative visionary behind the Pete Davidson-led Peacock series Bupkis, but plot details have yet to be announced. Possibly because those details threaten to turn the new film into something bearing scant resemblance to the original.

You’ve Got Mail, itself a remake of 1940’s The Shop Around the Corner (starring Jimmy Stewart and Margaret Sullavan), is centered around Kathleen Kelly (Ryan), an idealistic Upper West Side independent bookstore owner, and Joe Fox (Hanks), the cynical scion of a Barnes & Noble-like bookstore dynasty. The pair meet anonymously in an AOL chatroom, those early precursors to social media, and strike up a tastefully flirty friendship that drives them to consider leaving their current romantic partners (Greg Kinnear and Parker Posey, respectively). The dynamics of their quasi-courtship change, however, when Fox realizes his unnamed potential paramour is actually the woman his new store on the Upper West Side is about to put out of business. It’s a Montagues-and-Capulets-caliber obstacle that forestalls the inevitable happy ending.

The plot of this warm blanket of a movie hinges on two intertwined ideas: that strangers can connect over the internet and not turn out to be creeps, and that enormous chain bookstores are the mortal enemy of independents. Both ideas now seem quaintly, adorably naive.

Dating? On the internet??

In 1998, the internet was a mysterious novelty. Only 41% of adults had even logged on at all. While early adopters swore it would eventually change everything, most Americans were still wrapping their heads around the concept of email. Now, of course, the internet is the infrastructure modern society is built upon, and the filter through which many people experience the world. About 97% of adults younger than 50 are now connected to it at all times through smartphones, a technology that was nearly a decade away when You’ve Got Mail was made.

In retrospect, it’s a miracle that a person of Nora Ephron’s age—she was 56 at the time—perfectly depicted the moment when meeting strangers on the internet first broached mainstream acceptability. Prior to then, meeting people online was considered sordid, shameful business. Ephron both grounded her film in that perception and circumvented it by having her two leads fall ass-backward into internet romance.

There was something interesting and even sort of sweet about the idea of potential soulmates accidentally finding each other within the randomness of a non-sexual Web 1.0 chatroom. It now sounds like the kind of meet-cute one of those elderly couples in the Ephron-penned When Harry Met Sally might share if that film came out today.

What could possibly be an organic way for two attached people in 2026, though, to accidentally strike up a relationship online that retains the innocent curiosity of the 1998 internet? 

There’s nothing interesting anymore about meeting someone online. A chance encounter with a stranger on the r/Pringles subreddit could potentially lead to a hookup, which is something everyone has known or at least intuited for a very long time. Internet dating is now well past mainstream status. It’s something so pervasive as to no longer require any hand-wringing or soul-searching—you either do it or don’t do it, and nobody cares much either way. According to a 2019 study from Stanford University, over 39% of heterosexual couples now meet online, making the internet the most popular destination for sparking a new relationship.

But even if the filmmakers found a plausible scenario in which the two leads chastely meet online, they won’t face the dilemma that occupies the first half of the original movie—whether to physically meet someone who digitally swept you off your feet. After multiple decades of normalized internet dating, that question no longer carries any tension. Without it, the remake will just be about whether two people in unfulfilling relationships should turn their emotional infidelity into something more—essentially the plot of any generic romantic comedy.

Borders: Now there’s a name I haven’t heard in a long time

Although You’ve Got Mail correctly portrays the two leads’ ongoing anonymity as a red flag, the mutual identity firewall makes sense given the pair’s hesitation to go any further. But the idea that both parties in a more modern online flirtation would emotionally invest several months in someone who insists on keeping their identity a secret is ludicrous.

Even harder to pull off in a modern update than keeping their identities secret is who the two main characters actually are offline.

In 1998, an indie bookseller going up against a big-box bookstore would have been a genuine David-and-Goliath conflict. Barnes & Noble and Borders represented an existential threat to any local shop who struggled to keep up with the bottomless inventory, discounted pricing, and piping hot coffee those chains had in spades. Little did either side know they’d soon be united together in a battle for brick-and-mortar bookstore survival against Amazon, which launched just three years before You’ve Got Mail.

Now, all bookstores are fighting for their lives, with Barnes & Noble cribbing notes from indie bookshops to stay relevant in the BookTok era. (Borders did not survive Amazon’s ascendance, having reached its final chapter back in 2011.)

Affinity for independent booksellers was no match for the convenience and savings of a Barnes & Noble back in 1998, which is why Kelly eventually loses her shop in the film. That’s no longer necessarily the case. Anyone setting foot in a bookshop now has generally made an intentional choice to not buy a book from Amazon for cheap, and to instead experience human curation and customer service while supporting a local business. Meanwhile, Barnes & Noble is now more likely to buy a struggling independent bookshop than put one out of business.

The only way the major conflict in You’ve Got Mail would work in a modern update is if the plot moved out of the book world entirely, which is what will likely happen. But current options for a David-and-Goliath-esque business conflict that poignantly capture a changing world, mid-transformation, aren’t exactly inspiring. Maybe it will involve a celebrity podcaster at a major network launching a new show with the exact same idea as a well-established indie podcast—a concept I’m already mad about just having thought of. Maybe it will be the creator of a hot new AI chatbot financially ruining the founder of a once-great search engine. It might even be something even dumber. Unfortunately, the resulting movie could accidentally provide some incisive metacommentary about the moment “enshittification” came for Hollywood. 

Whatever happens, any remake of You’ve Got Mail that’s even vaguely faithful to the source material will have a title that no longer has any meaning, a premise that no longer matters, and a conflict that no longer exists. 

The only way to fix these problems would be to change so much about the original that what’s mainly being remade is the definition of what can reasonably be considered a remake. At that point, why not just start from scratch? The resounding box office lesson of 2026 is that audiences are tired of being treated like seals who reliably clap at the dangled fish of familiar IP. Original hits like Obsession, You Can See Everything, and The Drama inspired as much conversation this year as they did box office returns. 

Unrecognizable remakes of beloved classics, on the other hand, seem more like the modern descendants of another relic of the late 1990s: the straight-to-video sequel.

#10395. How to Build an Accessible Customer Reviews Section with HTML and CSS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Customer reviews are often displayed on business websites, but presenting them effectively requires more than adding a few star icons and customer quotes. Developers need to consider semantic HTML, responsive layouts, accessibility, and how review content fits into the overall user experience.

A well-built review section makes customer feedback easy to read without distracting visitors from the rest of the page. It should also work across different screen sizes and remain understandable to people using assistive technologies.

Let's look at how to build one using standard HTML and CSS.

The first step is to structure review content properly. Instead of placing everything inside generic

elements, use meaningful HTML elements to describe the content.

For example, a review can use

as its container and
for the customer's actual feedback.

This structure separates the review from its attribution and gives the section a clear heading. The rating also includes an accessible label so screen-reader users can understand what the stars represent.

For real websites, developers should display genuine customer feedback and avoid presenting invented testimonials as actual customer experiences.

A review section might look attractive on a desktop but become difficult to read on smaller screens. CSS Grid provides a straightforward way to create a flexible layout without relying on JavaScript.

The auto-fit and minmax() combination allows cards to adjust to the available space. Instead of defining a fixed number of columns for every device, the browser fits as many cards as the container can comfortably accommodate.

Developers working with more complex interfaces can explore SitePoint's guide to responsive web design for additional layout techniques.

A responsive layout should remain readable when viewed on a phone. Avoid fixed card widths, excessive padding, and text sizes that force users to zoom.

You can also adjust spacing at smaller viewport widths:

Test the section at several viewport sizes rather than relying on one desktop preview. Check that long customer names wrap correctly, cards do not overflow, and text remains comfortable to read.

Some review components use animated sliders, automatic scrolling, or hover effects. These features can create problems for visitors who prefer reduced motion or navigate with a keyboard.

A simple approach is to avoid unnecessary animation. If transitions are included, respect the visitor's system preference:

The MDN guide to using media queries for accessibility explains how developers can adapt interfaces to user preferences.

Also make sure interactive controls have visible keyboard focus styles. A carousel should provide usable previous and next controls, clear labels, and a way to pause automatic movement if it is used.

On a production website, reviews may come from a database, a content management system, or an external review service. Keeping the content separate from the presentation makes the component easier to maintain.

Businesses can also use an online reputation management platform to monitor customer feedback and understand how their brand is perceived across online channels.

For example, a developer could store each review with fields such as:

The frontend can then render the same component for every review. This avoids manually creating separate HTML for each customer and makes future design changes easier.

Developers should also validate incoming data, handle missing fields, and avoid displaying private customer information without permission.

Before publishing, check the component in different browsers and screen sizes. Test keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, text wrapping, and color contrast. If reviews are loaded dynamically, check how the section behaves when there are no reviews or when the data request fails.

A useful review component does not need complicated animations or a large JavaScript library. Semantic HTML, flexible CSS Grid layouts, accessible labels, and reliable content handling provide a strong foundation.

Customer feedback can only be useful on a website when visitors can understand and navigate it easily. By treating reviews as a proper interface component rather than decorative content, developers can create sections that are maintainable, accessible, and consistent with the rest of the website.

Terafab’s procurement team reportedly has already been to Japan, asking some toolmakers to deliver within months.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk’s Terafab, a joint venture of Tesla and SpaceX, has informally told equipment makers it is seeking to produce 1 million wafers per month after 2032, according to Financial News. About 70% of this output, or 700,000 wafers, is planned to go to memory, with more than 300,000 going to logic chips. Terafab’s procurement team has already visited Japan to ask some local toolmakers for delivery within months. The memory allotment would rival Samsung’s estimated DRAM production capacity if it were all of that type.

Samsung’s DRAM capacity was estimated last year at 650,000–700,000 wafers a month, while SK hynix is reportedly at about 550,000, with about 1 million a goal by 2030. The comparison has to be taken in context, as Terafab’s 700,000 measures all of its expected memory output, which could be NAND or DRAM, while the Samsung and SK hynix figures measure only DRAM. As it is, the memory portion alone would be 3.5 times the reported 200,000 at SK hynix’s Wuxi fab in China.

Many in the industry were skeptical when Musk announced the plans in March, but orders are now leading more companies to see a real business opportunity. The timeline is aggressive, as it usually takes three years or more to get from planning to volume at a leading-edge fab, and Terafab is targeting volume production in the second half of 2028. Procurement officials from the company reportedly visited Japan earlier this month to meet local suppliers and to work on details on bringing in equipment, with some suppliers asked to deliver within a few months.

The Elec also reports that Terafab representatives visited booths of about 10 Korean materials, parts, and equipment firms at SEMICON West, with some NDAs signed.

Logic chips are one thing — Jiji Press reports Terafab is working with Intel to adopt its 2nm and 1.4nm processes — but memory is another, and it’s not clear what type of memory is on the docket. Technical help from a Taiwanese company is under consideration for memory, but no partner has been named, leaving 70% of the planned wafers without a disclosed process technology.

Memory production tends to split between DRAM and NAND flash, the latter for non-volatile storage. A Tesla job listing for a Terafab Memory Process Integration Engineer, reported in August, covers end-to-end DRAM process integration and DRAM node development, and supports emerging memories such as MRAM, RRAM, and 3D DRAM. Terafab hasn’t said how its DRAM would be divided among products like HBM and LPDDR, both useful for AI and both mentioned in its job postings, or whether it expects to make and stack the DRAM itself or package chips it brings in.

Building a cutting-edge logic fab on U.S. soil is its own challenge, and Tesla and SpaceX lack chip-manufacturing experience. Even Musk, on a SpaceX call last month, called Terafab’s dates “very aggressive” and said he put “big error bars” on the timeline. The first SRAM test chip is targeted for around May or June 2027 at the Austin research facility.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

How TSMC might fit in remains open. TSMC says any fab with its involvement has to be run by TSMC, while Musk said his own companies would build and operate Terafab, a scenario which could leave TSMC as a space tenant. At least the spending plans are known: $16.8 billion for the first phase in Grimes County, Texas, with total investment of up to $119 billion if later phases proceed. A pilot plant could be completed as early as July 2027.

#10391. Jensen Huang brought a lot more to Nvidia than a cult of personality. Why his downfall hits so hard

By now, you have probably heard: Nvidia’s cofounder Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he confirmed having an affair. The woman at the center of it all, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a Chinese spy, in what sounds like a page ripped from a James Bond thriller. Reports now suggest that Huang also had at least two other affairs with employees at Nvidia.

The scandal is rife with intrigue and all-too-real consequences—including national security concerns and a major hit to the financial markets, as Nvidia’s share price continues to fall.

NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) was down about 5% in afternoon trading on Thursday at the time of this writing, after suffering double digit losses over the past few days since the scandal broke.

Altogether, the developments shine a spotlight on Huang’s unique geopolitical value, as he—and his AI chips—sat at the center of the U.S. AI arms race with China. Nvidia controls about 90% of the advanced chips market used for AI, per The New York Times.

His departure is a big loss for Nvidia—one that goes beyond his outsized personality, which made him one of tech’s biggest media darlings.

It also goes beyond his close proximity to President Donald Trump, who earlier this week defended and praised Huang for doing a “fantastic job.” (Reports allege that Trump knew about Huang’s affair: According to The Washington Post, Trump was briefed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio about the situation on May 12 on Air Force One, and The New York Times reported Trump was briefed about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s ‘close relationship’ as early as October 2025. Trump, for his part, denied hearing about the situation in May.)

“Sadly, greatness doesn’t guarantee goodness. It’s disappointing,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X. “The Economist says ‘no one is irreplaceable.’ They are very wrong.”

Huang’s value comes not only from the fact that he built and co-founded Nvidia—and remains the company’s largest individual shareholder—but also from his close personal and business ties and connections in Asia, with, among others, semiconductor maker TSMC and its founder Morris Chang, which has contributed to a massive supply chain pipeline for Nvidia.

Another issue: Huang’s departure from Nvidia comes at a critical political moment, on the heels of the Democratic party’s so-called “blue tsunami” sweep into Congress in last week’s midterm elections, which ushers in a new era for Silicon Valley—and could likely bring an abrupt end to its cozy relationship with Washington’s Republicans.

“Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk,” Democratic leader Senator Chuck Schumer posted on X Thursday. “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?”

#10390. How the effects of Jensen Huang’s ouster is spiraling out through the economy

NVIDIA and Jensen Huang aren’t the only ones in the crosshairs. 

Jensen Huang has had a bad week. It all began when news surfaced that he’d been having an affair with an alleged spy for the Chinese government. In response, NVIDIA’s corporate board began an investigation, and the FBI launched a probe, too. Then, late last night, news broke that Huang had at least one other affair, with a company executive who reported directly to him. By Thursday morning, Huang had resigned, and the chip company had appointed a new interim CEO. Reuters then reported a second affair with a different employee.

Obviously, this is bad news for NVIDIA. Stocks are down, and Democrats, now preparing to take back Congress, appear to be ramping up plans to investigate the company and any possible risks to US national security. But this is also bad for a range of other entities that have a stake in NVIDIA’s success.

Here are a few entities that stand to feel some of the blowback. 

The White House

The White House, fresh off a devastating loss in the midterm Congressional elections, stands to face questions about why it held off on taking action after it learned about Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy. The Trump administration already had a poor reputation for security and intelligence practices, but seemingly sleeping on this knowledge is all but certain to raise the prospect of further probes. 

Trump officials, notably, have cleared deals allowing NVIDIA to sell advanced computer chips to the US government, and even leveraged its influence over the company’s chips in geopolitical negotiations. 

Current and prospective NVIDIA customers

The US AI supply chain runs on NVIDIA. OpenAI, Anthropic, and a slew of other large language model developers rely on the company’s hardware. Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are also major customers. This is, in large part, because GPUs—or graphics processing units—are particularly adept at the kinds of computations needed to develop large reasoning models. 

Now, with so much scrutiny on NVIDIA, there’s a risk those companies—and any deals in progress—might face headwinds as the still-scrambling board figures out what to do next. The Semiconductor Industry Association, a major trade group that advocates for chip companies, declined to comment. Hugging Face, an AI developer that agreed to an acquisition by NVIDIA earlier this year, did not respond to a request for comment. 

Huang, notably, doesn’t seem to have had a succession plan, and reportedly had 60 direct reports instead. Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, was appointed interim CEO on Thursday morning. 

The scandal and disarray, of course, isn’t just bad for American companies that need NVIDIA’s chips. Given the extent to which Jensen Huang advocated for loosening chip sale limits to China, any customers with suspected links to the Chinese government may also see far more scrutiny on NVIDIA deals than before. 

U.S. federal agencies

The U.S. government is a major supporter of NVIDIA. The US government has also signed plenty of deals to use Nvidia on its own systems, including classified networks. The latest scandal is not only embarrassing for the US government, but raises concerns about the extent to which government officials were aware of the affair, and how they might have influenced the company’s dealings with federal agencies it works with. One former federal chief information told Fast Company that the scandal raises suspicions that the US security clearance system, which is supposed to engage in continuous monitoring, isn’t as up to snuff as it should be. 

Everyone else 

We really are that dependent on NVIDIA. If we learned anything from the chip shortage we experienced during the pandemic, the semiconductor market is remarkably concentrated, and disruptions with just one company can quickly ripple through the economy. In 2020, it was companies like TSMC, a Taiwan-based contract manufacturer that supplies chips for a host of devices. And the stock market—including pensions funds and 401ks—are deeply exposed to Nvidia stock.

“It is striking that NVIDIA, a $4 trillion company central to both the AI economy and US equity markets, appears to have no publicly identified successor to Jensen Huang,” Ann Lewis, a technology executive and former US government tech official, told Fast Company Wednesday. ‘In cybersecurity, we call this a single point of failure. A company of this scale should not depend so completely on one person’s relationships and judgment.”

#10388. Going deep on local AI performance benchmarking with Apple’s Mac Studio with M5 Ultra taking on Nvidia DGX Spark

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Is a Mac Studio a better investment than a DGX Spark?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Apple’s updated Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra SoC has already proven itself as one of the most powerful systems around, thanks to its 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators for the matrix math operations that drive AI compute. Beyond that raw power, options for up to 512GB of unified memory have many local AI enthusiasts lining up for the 13 to 15 weeks it’ll take for Apple to ship one right now.

But is our tested Mac Studio config worth a whopping $12,300 or more for those folks? We already tested the maxed-out M5 Ultra chip with the popular Qwen 3.8 27B in our initial review, but that compact dense model doesn’t come anywhere close to exercising 256GB of memory. We wanted to fill that pool to the brim with cutting-edge large models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash.

We also have some new benchmarks at our disposal to see how the Mac Studio stacks up in agentic tasks on the GPU side in the wake of our review of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. So there's much to dig into.

We started our more detailed local AI testing with Artificial Analysis' AgentPerf-Local benchmark. This test plays back recorded inference traces with certain models across a range of agentic AI workloads to gauge performance. Artificial Analysis provides a full breakdown of this workload, but the bulk of its work takes place in prompt processing rather than token generation. As a result, it should favor systems with lots of raw compute, which both GB10 and the M5 Ultra have at their disposal.

The M5 Ultra's 80-core GPU dwarfs GB10's 48 Blackwell SMs at a high level. Even without detailed info on clocks, it would be extremely difficult for GB10 to outgun the M5 Ultra in this test. And the Mac's 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth gives it just over four times as much decode bandwidth as GB10's 273 GB/s. But as our past tests have shown, raw specs aren't as important as delivered performance with AI. Delivered performance can vary greatly from paper specs.

We continued to use the dense Qwen 3.8 27B for this test. We used llama.cpp as our inference backend on both the Mac Studio and a single Dell Pro Precision GB10 box, which is nearly identical to the DGX Spark. We further enabled Qwen 3.8 27B’s native multi-token prediction (MTP) support for a decode speed boost on both platforms.

Versus a single DGX Spark-like system, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio finishes this agentic test in just under half the time, an extremely impressive result. One might think this is a silly comparison given the imbalance in compute resources and memory bandwidth between these two systems, but the cost of a single 4TB Dell Pro Precision GB10, like the one we tested, is now a whopping $10K, so comparing it to the $12K Mac Studio head-to-head isn’t actually that far-fetched.

Because AgentPerf-Local performs a fixed amount of work on every system, we can also directly compare power efficiency between platforms by recording the wall power consumed by a single Spark and the Mac Studio and converting it to task energy in kilojoules.

At least with llama.cpp, the Mac Studio not only finishes the AgentPerf-Local test much faster than the DGX Spark, but it also consumes less task energy overall — about 16% less. A different inference engine might produce a more favorable result for the Spark-like system, but apples-to-apples, this test looks fantastic for the Mac Studio.

We can multiply both task time and energy consumed (in kilojoules) together to arrive at the energy-delay product (EDP) for each system. A lower EDP wraps up a fast time to completion and a low task energy into a single comparable figure for efficiency.

The Mac Studio’s EDP is under half that of the DGX Spark in this test, once again indicating its impressive efficiency and performance with this dense model and workload.

Of course, Qwen 3.8 27B doesn’t need 256GB (or even 128GB) of RAM to do its thing. To really stretch the legs of the Mac Studio, we chose two larger open models that are near the top of capability benchmarks right now: GLM-5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017.

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio can natively fit quantized versions of these models (a four-bit quantization in the case of GLM 5.3 and a two-bit quantization courtesy of Unsloth for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) in its 256GB of RAM, but there’s no way even those quantizations will fit on a single 128GB DGX Spark.

That’s where the clustering capability of Nvidia’s platform comes in. We’ve already seen how pairing up Sparks can scale up one’s local inference capacity, and that capability is critical when evaluating them against a Mac Studio like this.

But the rapidly rising prices of GB10 systems have frustrated our value analysis during the course of this testing. For just one example, Lenovo set all of its ThinkStation PGX systems to a “coming soon” status during our tests. And as we’ve already mentioned, the Dell Pro Precision GB10s we’re clustering here are an eye-popping $10K each. We have no reason to believe the rest of the GB10 systems on the market will be that much cheaper once this current volatility shakes out.

No matter how you slice it, getting even a pair of DGX Sparks with 4TB SSDs is going to end up costing quite a bit more than this single Mac Studio, even if $20K for a dual-Dell cluster is at the top end of the market. $15K or more is a relatively more reasonable benchmark, but even then, that’s 25% more money than a single M5 Ultra Studio.

We don't yet have end-to-end agentic tests for these larger models, but directionally, we can still consider prompt processing and decode performance to see which of these systems would deliver faster agentic turnaround.

Because of the limited choice of compatible inference engines for Apple Silicon, we have to use llama.cpp for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. Worse, the Mac Studio can't hold both the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 model weights and the DSpark speculative decoding model required to boost token output even with a two-bit quantization, so we’re forced to leave performance on the table.

In contrast, the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serving recipe for our Spark cluster can take advantage of DSpark speculative decoding and the TensorFold inference engine, which can deliver higher performance than llama.cpp.

Even with MLX support, llama.cpp performance with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the Mac Studio is pokey next to the DGX Spark cluster. Between its slower prompt processing speed and unaugmented decoding, it would end up at a disadvantage in agentic work with this model.

The community two-Spark serving recipe from Mia’s AI Lab with TensorFold is a major asset for owners of those systems, even accounting for the bit of extra work involved in setting up and managing a Spark cluster.

Where the Mac running llama.cpp needs anywhere from 10 to 25 minutes to digest the longest context lengths we tested for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the Spark cluster needs under five minutes at most to do the same jobs with this recipe — and the TensorFold inference engine is much faster on the decode side, too. If you want to run this model locally, a pair of Sparks is the clear winner right now.

With DeepSeek out of the way, let’s consider GLM 5.3 Flash, another leading open model for local intelligence. Because MTP with GLM 5.3 Flash doesn't require a separate drafting model, we can give it a decode boost on the Mac Studio without the memory headroom issues we saw with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. For our Spark cluster, we chose to run GLM 5.3 Flash using a recipe cooked up by Mia's AI Lab.

GLM 5.3 Flash runs much better on llama.cpp than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash does, but even so, the DGX Spark cluster delivers much faster prompt processing times across the board. The M5 Ultra's memory bandwidth advantage means the Mac is delivering higher tokens per second on the decode side, but it’s likely that any agentic turn would still finish faster on the Spark cluster.

Because a TensorFold serving recipe is available for GLM 5.3 Flash on Apple Silicon, however, we can see just how much extra performance is available from an MLX-specific four-bit model quantization and a theoretically higher-performance inference engine.

This serving recipe turbocharges the Mac Studio’s performance compared to llama.cpp. Prompt processing times with TensorFold get much closer to those of the Spark cluster, and decode throughput is a startling three times faster, on average.

We expect (and can only hope) that improved inference engine support and serving recipes for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on the M5 Ultra will arrive in time as community members unleash their coding agents on this hardware, because the performance potential is clearly there for Apple Silicon.

A single M5 Ultra Mac Studio can deliver incredible local AI performance and power efficiency versus a single DGX Spark when all the puzzle pieces fall into place. And that's not as absurd a comparison as it might seem.

Prices for unified memory systems are ballooning to the point that a single Dell Pro Precision GB10 system with a 4TB SSD is now over $10K, closing in on the $12K-ish price of the Mac Studio configuration that we tested. We expect those trends will only continue as the RAM and NAND supply crunch becomes more acute.

But our broader experience shows that the M5 Ultra's impressive performance isn't assured from every model and inference engine, especially from the bigger and highly intelligent models you'll want to put in 256GB of RAM.

This Mac's prompt processing speeds can really rip with llama.cpp and smaller models like Qwen 3.8 27B, but you really want to ensure that you have a higher-performance serving recipe at your disposal for bigger models like GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. The TensorFold engine runs GLM 5.3 Flash incredibly well, but it doesn’t support DeepSeek at all yet.

As we emphasized in our review of the M4 Max Mac Studio, memory bandwidth is just one factor in AI inference performance. You need to take the entire hardware-software stack into account in order to wholly judge the performance and model compatibility available from these extremely pricey unified memory setups.

Even as Apple closes the performance shortfalls of its hardware for AI inference, development and support around the MLX stack has a ways to go before it catches up with the maturity and performance, as well as the model and inference engine options, available on Nvidia hardware.

The enduring value of the DGX Spark platform beyond its raw performance and scalability is that the breadth and velocity of community software development and support around the platform has gotten to the point that you're virtually assured of a way to run a hot new model soon after its weights hit Hugging Face (at least assuming you have enough Sparks to cluster to provide the memory capacity necessary).

That assurance of community software support and ongoing development, along with the DRAM and NAND supply crunches, means high demand and ever higher prices for 128GB GB10 boxes. Two such Sparks with 4TB drives will run you an eye-watering $15K to $20K+, depending on the partner system and storage configuration you choose. And those prices are likely to continue rising, making a single Mac Studio a potentially appealing option as long as Apple doesn’t jack up its prices for these systems in turn.

If strong local AI performance is just one thing you need from a personal workstation, and you also want one of the world's fastest CPUs and a powerful GPU for general-purpose work in one well-rounded, efficient, and quiet compact chassis, the Mac Studio is a remarkable system.

If you can wait for software to catch up to this system’s incredible performance potential for local AI and don’t mind the possibility of narrower model and inference engine support compared to a DGX Spark setup, get in line, as lead times for these systems stretch into February 2027 as of this writing.

But if you're thinking about dropping well over $10K specifically for the purpose of building a local AI inference setup right now, perhaps for yourself or a small office, clustering a pair of Sparks gets you both the memory capacity and compute horsepower you need with the robust software support and broad model compatibility you’d expect for that outlay to be worthwhile. Those assurances may be worth the lower raw performance potential of such a cluster compared to the Mac Studio.

As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

#10386. Trump’s suggestion for the next Nvidia CEO is another tech titan he’s already close with

With Jensen Huang officially out as president and CEO of Nvidia, rumors are swirling over who will take his place at the helm of one of the world’s biggest tech companies. Could it be interim CEO Colette Kress, who’s spent more than a decade as Nvidia’s executive vice president and CFO? Or maybe the company’s cofounder Chris Malachowsky, now a senior vice president of engineering and operations?

President Donald Trump has a different idea. His left-field pick: former Apple CEO Tim Cook. In a post on Truth Social, Trump announced his preference for Huang’s successor.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

Beyond Trump’s dubious claim that Huang did “a fantastic job” as CEO—having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy might disqualify him from that distinction—Cook is far from an obvious pick to step into the role.

It was just months ago in September that Cook stepped away from being Apple’s CEO and became its executive chairman. In a company meeting announcing the decision, Cook said his stepdown had to come at a time when “business had to be doing great,” when the “product road map to be incredible,” and when his replacement, former senior vice president of hardware engineering John Ternus, was “ready for the role.” With all those conditions met, “now was the time,” Cook said.

Why, then, would Trump want Cook to take on another CEO mantle? Notably, the two have gotten close during Trump’s second term as president.

Trump and Cook, sitting in a tree

Trump and Cook weren’t always buddies. During Trump’s first term as president, he infamously referred to Cook as “Tim Apple,” seemingly forgetting his name.

But since Trump took back the office in 2025, Cook has frequently been spotted at Trump’s side, from attending a White House dinner for tech CEOs last September to watching an early screening of First Lady Melania Trump’s documentary in early 2026.

For his part, Cook insists that he’s not politically aligned with Trump, instead abstaining from politics entirely.

“What I do is I interact on policy, not politics. I’m not a political person on either side. I’m not political,” Cook said in an interview for Good Morning America earlier this year. “I’m kind of straight down the middle. And I focus on policy, so I’m very pleased that the president and the administration is accessible to talk about policy,” he added.

That purported focus on policy aligns with Cook’s intentions for his role as Apple’s executive chairman, which include overseeing the company’s global relations. “This is an area where we’ve built relationships over multiple years and a decade-plus, and I think I can help with that,” Cook said when announcing his stepdown.

#10383. New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

One ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In recent months, high-profile headlines about AI models letting loose from their safeguards dominated headlines. Now, the Frontier Model Forum (FMF) has released a new Jailbreak Rating Framework that aims to track how easy it might be for a given AI model to get around safeguards. The framework also estimates the scale of the collateral damage, should an AI model wreak cyber-havoc across the internet.

The project started in 2023 with the support of four founding companies: Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. The published Jailbreak Rating Framework is a rough analog to the well-known CVSS security rating system, but specifically targeted at classifying the type and severity of LLM jailbreaks across various axes and multiple frontier LLM providers.

Many AI companies and evaluation entities already have their own rating systems, but the FMF intends for its scale to be a cross-vendor standard that teams developing patches can rely on.

The FMF's approach is to have a classification method for jailbreaks that can make a model perform cyber-warfare operations beyond what's already out, across both the regular and black market. Version 1.0 of the proposal is a work-in-progress, and the group is taking comments and suggestions on it until December 21, noting that relying on its system in the meantime is inadvisable.

Right now, the framework has four scoring components, split across two main categories: severity, measuring how serious a jailbreak technique is, and likelihood, or how easy it is to find and weaponize it.

A combined final rating adds the scores obtained from the two categories into a final low-to-critical rating. The scientists note that the capability gain is the most important dimension and acts as both a floor and a ceiling for the remaining scores — a jailbreak that doesn't offer results beyond what can already be obtained via other means is meaningless within the purview of the grading system.

The individual ratings pertain to capability gains, capability scope, ease of deployment, and ease of discovery. They're all graded from zero to three, though the FMF stresses that a rating of zero doesn't mean a jailbreak is harmless or ought to be ignored — rather, it means the flaw should be addressed by standard practices like the platform's policies and standard cybersecurity ratings.

An important feature is that the FMF's baseline implicitly changes as models evolve, meaning that a grade of zero for a jailbreak in 2026 likely isn't going to mean the same thing as it would in 2028, or isn't better than alternative tools. A capability-gain rating of zero means that the jailbreak under analysis doesn't offer any improvement beyond what can already be done with existing models or tooling right off the bat.

For example, jailbreaking a model to perform a DDoS on a site isn't all that helpful to an attacker, since there are a number of black-market sites for that — or even other LLMs with fewer safeguards. This doesn't mean the jailbreak isn't handy, only that it's no better than the alternatives. However, the rating can be higher if the attacker can leverage the jailbreak to get a better DDoS than they could otherwise shop for.

On the other end of the capability-gain scale, three means that a jailbroken model can perform cyber-attacks with capabilities similar to those of a model operating without safeguards.

The capability scope measurement is easier to interpret: zero means that the jailbreak only works for one specific action or target and can't be tweaked for other applications, or in other words, is a one-trick pony. A jailbreak gets a rating of three when it can, without specific redesign, make a model perform work across at least two entirely unrelated categories of cyber-warfare — like getting the model to both autonomously discover vulnerabilities or, separately, write malware.

For ease of deployment, the FMF considers the amount of human interaction, or the degree of automation that the jailbreak allows. A zero means that the jailbreak must be steered by humans with a high degree of knowledge, providing additional instructions to be effective, while a three means that, with little effort, it can be used by a novice and results in an automated cyber-warfare task.

Last but by no means least, ease-of-discovery is how hard it is to find the jailbreak. At a zero, the attacker must spend copious amounts of money on inference tokens, need elevated access (like a privileged account given to a white-hat hacker), or specialized infrastructure like a legion of AI servers. A rating of three simply means that anyone can look up the technique and use it.

If all of this sounds familiar, you may be thinking of Anthropic's safeguard-breakage classifiers the company proposed in July 2026, after an incident that led to Claude Fable 5 being temporarily unavailable. Much like the FMF's effort, Anthropic's system would also use a moving baseline and only consider jailbreaks that improve on cyber-warfare capabilities already available.

That document is strikingly similar to FMF's proposal. Anthropic is an FMF founding member, and as such may have had a hand or two in developing the new standard — though we have no confirmation either way.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

#10382. Build a Hardware Diagnostic Log with Vanilla JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

A device disconnects halfway through a test. The application reports a timeout, the firmware restarts, and the next attempt succeeds. Where should you start?

For developers working with connected devices, browser interfaces, or hardware prototypes, an application error is often only the final symptom. Replacing code without recording the conditions around a failure can leave you chasing the wrong layer.

This tutorial builds a small browser-based diagnostic log. It records measurements, preserves the test conditions, and exports evidence for another developer to review. You need basic HTML and JavaScript knowledge; no framework or connected instrument is required.

1. Define the question before collecting data Consider a hypothetical development board that disconnects when a peripheral starts. Several explanations remain possible: a firmware exception, a transport problem, or a power supply issue. Start with a testable question: “Does the measured supply voltage change when this peripheral starts?” That question tells you what to record and what to keep constant.

Use a known-good board of the same revision where available. Match the firmware, cable, supply, peripheral, and workload. A comparison loses value when several conditions change together.

Record the observation separately from the explanation:

The hypothesis remains provisional. A reading taken after the device restarts does not establish what happened during the failure.

2. Choose evidence that answers the question Application logs, firmware traces, and bench measurements answer different questions. A timeout establishes that an operation did not finish in time; it does not identify a failed component.

For a view of specialist equipment used in phone-board troubleshooting, DIYFIXTOOL’s overview of Chip-Level Diagnostic Tools discusses thermal imaging, BGA X-ray inspection, and inductance testing. Treat it as a vendor-authored introduction to equipment categories; use instrument documentation and board-specific references when interpreting measurements.

The log below deliberately leaves interpretation to the operator. Enter a numeric value, its unit, and the conditions under which it was measured. Do not turn an isolated reading into an automatic “faulty chip” verdict.

For physical measurements, follow the board and instrument documentation and work within your training. This tutorial covers the software record rather than a procedure for probing or repairing a powered device. 3. Build a small, accessible form

Save the following as index.html and serve it through your usual local development server. For example, if Python is installed, run python -m http. server 8000 in its directory, then open http://localhost:8000. 4. Preserve data without hiding failures

The application stores an array of records as JSON. On reload, it parses that JSON and checks the expected field types before rendering it. Parsing alone does not validate the structure of stored data.

SitePoint’s guide to looping through JSON responses provides useful background on working with objects and arrays after parsing JSON. Each table cell uses textContent, so a note containing HTML is displayed as text rather than inserted as markup. The MDN documentation for textContent explains this behavior.

Storage operations sit inside try...catch blocks because browser persistence can fail. The interface keeps new measurements in memory and offers an export when saving fails. It does not claim those measurements will survive a reload. For another practical vanilla JavaScript project, SitePoint’s **Markdown previewer tutorial **explores browser UI construction and persistence.

As **MDN’s localStorage documentation **explains, storage belongs to the document’s origin. Opening the application on a different port may therefore show a different log. This prototype is a single-browser tool, so export important sessions and avoid recording customer identifiers or private device contents.

5. Compare measurements under matching conditions Suppose two hypothetical readings are 3.29 V and 3.08 V. Their difference is −0.21 V. That arithmetic is straightforward; its meaning depends on the rail specification, measurement uncertainty, workload, and timing.

Do not add a universal voltage threshold to the application. A device-specific limit should come from its specification or an established test procedure.

If the failure is brief, a manually entered steady-state measurement may miss it entirely. Record that limitation. The next investigation may require a time-correlated capture rather than another static reading.

When sharing a session, include the firmware revision, board revision, instrument settings, and reproduction steps. A colleague should be able to repeat the comparison without guessing how the reading was obtained. 6. Verify the workflow before relying on it Try adding a decimal reading and a negative reading, then reload the page. Confirm that both values and their units remain intact. Enter a note containing test and check that it appears literally in the table.

Export the JSON and inspect the record count. Then simulate blocked storage and confirm that the interface reports the failure while allowing an export of the current session.

For a larger application, add editable entries, instrument metadata, and explicit baseline records. A shared service would also need access controls, server-side validation, and a policy for retention. These additions should follow the needs of the diagnostic workflow.

Turn a symptom into a reproducible investigation

The finished prototype captures a useful minimum: what was measured, where, when, and under which conditions. Its value comes from preserving evidence that another person can inspect.

When an application error crosses into firmware or hardware, that record helps you choose the next experiment. Repeat the failure, change one variable, and document what the new evidence supports before deciding what to fix.

#10381. A major change to the U.S. mortgage market could be coming. Here’s why homeowners should care

As President Donald Trump enters the lame-duck era of his presidency, that raises questions about which of his various agenda items will actually get accomplished.

One of his long-standing goals has been to end the government conservatorship that mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have been subject to since the financial crisis. After failing to make much headway during his first term in office, Trump revived those intentions for his second term—but once again hasn’t made it much of a priority.

This past May, Trump posted on Truth Social that he was “working on taking these amazing companies public,” while adding that the U.S. government would retain its mortgage guarantees and oversight role for both government-sponsored entities. But only a matter of days later, when asked about an initial public offering for Fannie and Freddie, Trump said: “It’s not a rush.”

Meanwhile, Trump has also seen an opportunity with the current government control of Fannie and Freddie to use them as tools to address affordability. On the eve of the midterm elections, he announced at a rally in Kansas that the entities would invest $4.3 billion in home loans in the state next year, which he promised would help 15,000 people achieve their American dream.

Removing Fannie and Freddie from conservatorship, experts have cautioned, could push up mortgage rates. And because Democrats regained control of Congress by campaigning on affordability, that may make them reluctant to entertain an end to this long-standing conservatorship now, when so many Americans are grappling with an affordability crisis. 

Further complicating matters is how, exactly, the Trump administration could go about ending the conservatorship—whether by an executive order or with support from Congress. Legal and political analysts are divided on whether that could happen or if Trump would need support from Congress, as Realtor.com reported.  

Frank Cassidy, the former Federal Housing Commissioner in Trump’s second term, told the outlet that Trump can privatize Fannie and Freddie without Republican control of Congress, but noted that how they were structured post-conservatorship would matter. 

“It hasn’t been a priority yet,” Cassidy told Realtor.com. “It would need to be worked on very quickly because it will take some time.” 

A PUSH FROM WALL STREET

One person who’d very much like privatizing Fannie and Freddie to be a priority is hedge funder Bill Ackman. He says that removing these entities from conservatorship would be “helpful” for improving housing affordability because it would remove any political uncertainty from the mortgage market, particularly if Democrats were to use Fannie and Freddie in the future to “achieve political objectives.”

Of course, he has an incentive at stake: His firm, Pershing Square, is invested in both Fannie and Freddie. Though the companies were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010, they have traded in the over-the-counter market ever since.

Still, Ackman argues that Americans stand to benefit from ending the conservatorship. “This is a major point of economic policy where the president can have a hundreds of billion-dollar win for the American people,” he told CNBC, adding that it could be a “windfall” to the tune of $500 billion.

WEIGHING THE CONSEQUENCES

Such optimism for a widespread benefit to Americans counters what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed on a 2Way podcast appearance last month. 

While he said that the Trump administration will tackle the ownership structure of Fannie and Freddie in either 2027 or 2028, he said the “north star” guiding a decision will be whether ending the conservatorship can be accomplished without meaningfully increasing the spread between mortgage-backed securities and Treasury yields.

“It’s unclear why homeowners or mortgage holders would benefit from a change in the arrangement of the shareholder structure,” Bessent said.

What people on both sides of the political aisle can agree on is that a rush to end an 18-year arrangement would be most problematic. Still, the clock is ticking on Trump’s time in office to accomplish this goal, with less than 800 days remaining. 

And one person who could stand in the way is Representative Maxine Waters, a Democrat from California, who is running to chair the House Financial Services Committee after serving on it for more than a decade. 

As Realtor.com reported, Waters has historically opposed any efforts to rapidly end the conservatorship without comprehensive congressional oversight. “To address the affordable housing crisis, Congress must ensure that Fannie and Freddie meet their mission to provide liquidity, sustainability, and affordability to all housing markets in the U.S., and at all times,” Waters said at a hearing in April.

#10380. I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

Unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

It’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without issue. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

It does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

Because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

The Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

On the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only issue I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

The homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

The buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

It’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

As far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.
